title: MAS2901: Statistical Inference
text:
What is Statistical Inference?
Statistical inference is the process of using data from a sample to learn about a population. Sometimes the population is concrete (e.g. “all people in the country today”). In other situations we want to generalise beyond those we sampled to a broader target population (sometimes called a superpopulation), such as “future patients with similar characteristics”. Clear definitions and sensible assumptions are essential for valid conclusions.
There are two main types of statistical inference:

Frequentist inference. Parameters are treated as fixed but unknown. Probability statements are about data we might observe under repeated sampling from the same model.
Bayesian inference. Parameters are treated as random with a prior distribution. Probability statements are about the parameter given the data via the posterior distribution.

The examples below are only to build intuition about the core difference between frequentist and Bayesian inference. Don’t worry about the details—we’ll cover them carefully later in the course.







Example 1 (A comparison of Frequentist vs Bayesian inference) A survey asks \(n=20\) students if they prefer study space \(A\) or \(B\).
Suppose \(x=12\) prefer \(A\). Compare a frequentist and a Bayesian estimate of the long-run proportion \(p\) who would choose \(A\).










TipSolution





Frequentist. The natural estimator is the sample proportion
\[
\hat p=\frac{x}{n}=\frac{12}{20}=0.60.
\]
Bayesian (with a uniform prior). Take a \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) prior for \(p\). The posterior is
\[
p \mid x \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1+x,\,1+n-x)=\mathrm{Beta}(13,9),
\]
whose mean is
\[
\mathbb{E}[p\mid x]=\frac{13}{13+9}=\frac{13}{22}\approx 0.591.
\]
Interpretation. The frequentist estimate \(\hat p\) is a function of the data and treats \(p\) as fixed.
The Bayesian estimate is an expectation of \(p\) itself under the posterior distribution.











Example 2 (Interpreting probability statements) Decide whether each statement is frequentist or Bayesian in spirit.

“If we repeated the survey many times, the method we use would produce intervals that capture \(p\) about \(95\%\) of the time.”

“Given the data from this survey and our prior, there is a \(95\%\) probability that \(p\) lies between \(0.45\) and \(0.75\).”











TipSolution






Frequentist. This describes long-run coverage of a procedure over repeated samples with \(p\) fixed.

Bayesian. This is a probability statement about \(p\) given the observed data (a credible interval).

1  Probability Theory
text:
The sample space \(\Omega\). all possible outcomes of an experiment.
Example: for a coin toss, \(\Omega = \{\text{Heads}, \text{Tails}\}\).

Events subsets of the sample space. We use capital letters \(A, B, \ldots\) to denote events.

The complement of \(A\) is \(A^c\), meaning \(A\) does not occur.

The intersection \(A \cap B\) means \(A\) and \(B\) occur.

The union \(A \cup B\) means \(A\) or \(B\) (or both) occur.


A probability distribution \(\mathrm{Pr}\). Assigns numbers between \(0\) and \(1\) to events, with \(\mathrm{Pr}(\Omega)=1\).









Definition 1.1 (Complement, Intersection and Union)  

Complement: \(A^c = \{x \in \Omega \mid x \notin A \}\).
Intersection: \(A\cap B = \{x \in \Omega \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}\).

Union: \(A\cup B = \{x \in \Omega \mid x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}\).


















Definition 1.2 (Addition rule (inclusion–exclusion)) For any two events \(A, B\subseteq \Omega\), we have \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \cup B) = \mathrm{Pr}(A) + \mathrm{Pr}(B) - \mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B).
\]











Example 1.1 (A quick inclusion–exclusion check) Roll a fair six-sided die. Let \(A=\{\text{even}\}\) and \(B=\{\text{number} \ge 4\}\). Compute \(\mathrm{Pr}(A\cup B)\).










TipSolution






Solution 1.1. We have

\(\mathrm{Pr}(A)=3/6=1/2\) (even outcomes \(2,4,6\)).

\(\mathrm{Pr}(B)=3/6=1/2\) (outcomes \(4,5,6\)).

\(\mathrm{Pr}(A\cap B)=2/6=1/3\) (outcomes \(4,6\)).

By inclusion–exclusion 1.2, \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A\cup B)=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{1}{3}=\tfrac{2}{3}.
\]











Definition 1.3 (Mutually Exclusive, Exhaustive Events, and Partitions)  

Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) if they cannot occur together: \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B) = 0.
\]
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are exhaustive if at least one of them must occur: \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \cup B) = 1.
\]
More generally, a collection of events \(\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}\) is exhaustive if \(\bigcup_{i=1}^k B_i = \Omega\), where \(\Omega\) is the sample space.
A collection of events \(\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}\) forms a partition of \(\Omega\) if they are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Equivalently,

\(B_i \cap B_j = \varnothing\) for all \(i \neq j\) (non-overlapping), and

\(\bigcup_{i=1}^k B_i = \Omega\) (their union is the whole sample space).


















Definition 1.4 (Conditional probability) If \(\mathrm{Pr}(B) > 0\), the probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
\]











Definition 1.5 (Independence) Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if knowing that one occurs does not change the probability of the other: \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B) = \mathrm{Pr}(A)\mathrm{Pr}(B).
\] Equivalently, \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A\mid B) = \mathrm{Pr}(A) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{Pr}(B\mid A) = \mathrm{Pr}(B)
\]











Theorem 1.1 (Law of Total Probability) If \(B_1,\dots,B_k\) form a partition 1.3 of the sample space (mutually exclusive and exhaustive events), then for any event \(A\): \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^k \mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B_i)\mathrm{Pr}(B_i).
\]










NoteProof






Proof 1.1. Since \(B_1\ldots, B_n\) form a partition of \(\Omega\), we can decompose any event \(A\) in a disjoint union of intersections: \[
A = \bigcup_{i=1}^n (A\cap B_i).
\] By induction on the addition rule 1.2, we thus have \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Pr}(A\cap B_i).
\] By the definition of conditional probability 1.4, we have \(\mathrm{Pr}(A\cap B_i) = \mathrm{Pr}(A\mid B_i) \mathrm{Pr}(B_i)\). Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{Pr}(A) =  \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B_i)\mathrm{Pr}(B_i).
\]

















Theorem 1.2 (Bayes’ Theorem) If \(\mathrm{Pr}(B) > 0\), then \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(B \mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
\]










NoteProof






Proof 1.2. From the definition of conditional probability 1.4,
\[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
\]
But the intersection \(A \cap B\) can also be written the other way round: \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B) = \mathrm{Pr}(B \cap A).
\]
Using the definition of conditional probability again, \[
\mathrm{Pr}(B \cap A) = \mathrm{Pr}(B \mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A).
\]
Substituting this into the first expression gives \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(B \mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
\]
This completes the proof.











Example 1.2 (Student Example) Seventy percent of students are attentive in lectures and thirty percent are not. If a student is attentive the probability of passing the course is \(0.8\). If a student is not attentive the probability of passing the course is \(0.1\).

A student is selected at random. What is the probability that they pass the course?
Given that the student passed the course, what is the probability that they were attentive?











TipSolution






Solution 1.2. Let

\(P\) denote the event of a student passing the course.
\(A\) denote the event of a student being attentive.
\(A^c\) denote the event of a student not being attentive.


Attentive and inattentive form a partition. By the law of total probability,

\[
\mathrm{Pr}(P)=\mathrm{Pr}(P\mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A)+\mathrm{Pr}(P\mid A^c)\mathrm{Pr}(A^c)=0.8\times0.7+0.1\times0.3=0.59.
\]

Using Bayes’ theorem,

\[
\mathrm{Pr}(A\mid P)=\frac{\mathrm{Pr}(P\mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A)}{\mathrm{Pr}(P)}
=\frac{0.8\times0.7}{0.59}=0.949\ \text{(3 s.f.)}.
\]

title: 1  Probability Theory
text:
1.2 Random Variables
We use upper-case letters for random variables, e.g. \(X, Y, X_1, X_2,\dots\).

Cumulative distribution function (cdf). For any (real-valued) random variable \(X\),
\[
F(x)=\mathrm{Pr}(X\le x).
\]
Discrete case (pmf). If \(X\) is discrete, its probability mass function is
\[
p(x)=\mathrm{Pr}(X=x),\qquad \sum_x p(x)=1.
\]
Continuous case (pdf). If \(X\) is continuous, its probability density function satisfies
\[
f(x)=\frac{\partial F(x)}{\partial x},\qquad \mathrm{Pr}(a<X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1.
\]








Example 1.3 (Discrete CDF.) Let \(X\) be the outcome of a fair six-sided die. Find \(p(x)\) and \(F(3)\).










TipSolution






Solution 1.3. \(p(x)=\mathrm{Pr}(X=x)=1/6\) for \(x\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\), and \(0\) otherwise.
\(F(3)=\mathrm{Pr}(X\le 3)=\mathrm{Pr}(\{1,2,3\})=3\times(1/6)=1/2.\)











Example 1.4 Let \(X\sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\). Compute \(\mathrm{Pr}(0.2<X<0.5)\).










TipSolution






Solution 1.4. Here \(f(x)=1\) for \(0<x<1\) and \(0\) otherwise.
\[
\mathrm{Pr}(0.2<X<0.5)=\int_{0.2}^{0.5} 1\,dx = 0.3.
\]





1.2.1 Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Densities
Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are random variables with joint PDF/PMF \(f_{XY}(x,y)\) (often written \(f(x,y)\)). From this joint distribution we can define:

Marginal distributions: the distribution of each variable on its own.

Conditional distributions: the distribution of one variable given the other.

Independence: the case where the joint factorises.








Definition 1.6 (Marginal Distributions) If we only care about \(X\), regardless of \(Y\), we integrate/sum out \(Y\): \[
f_X(x) = \int f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
\] Similarly for \(f_Y(y)\).
Note: knowing the marginals does not determine the joint.











Definition 1.7 (Conditional Densities) For \(y\) in the support of \(Y\) with \(f_Y(y) > 0\), we define: \[
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}.
\] This describes the distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=y\).











Theorem 1.3 (Law of Total Probability) We can recover the marginal by “averaging” the conditional over \(Y\): \[
f_X(x) = \int f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
\]











Definition 1.8 (Independence) \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if \[
f(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y).
\] In this case, \(f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = f_X(x)\): knowing \(Y\) tells us nothing about \(X\).

text:
1.3 Expectations, Variances and Covariances







Definition 1.9 (Expected Value) The expected value (or population mean) of \(X\) is \[
\mathrm{E}[X] =
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \sum_{\text{all } x} x\,p_X(x), & \text{if $X$ is discrete}, \\
\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, & \text{if $X$ is continuous}.
\end{cases}
\]
We often write \(\mu = \mathrm{E}[X]\). This is a measure of location.











Definition 1.10 (Expectation of \(g(X)\)) Let \(g(\cdot)\) be any function and \(X\) a random variable with PMF \(p_X\) (discrete) or PDF \(f_X\) (continuous). The expected value of \(g(X)\) is \[
\mathrm{E}[g(X)] =
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \sum_{\text{all } x} g(x)\,p_X(x), & \text{if $X$ is discrete},\\
\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, & \text{if $X$ is continuous}.
\end{cases}
\]











Definition 1.11 (Expectation (Bivariate)) If \((X,Y)\) is a pair of random variables with joint PMF \(p_{X,Y}\) (discrete) or joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}\) (continuous), then for any function \(g(x,y)\) \[
\mathrm{E}[g(X,Y)] =
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \sum_{\text{all } x}\sum_{\text{all } y} g(x,y)\,p_{X,Y}(x,y), & \text{if $(X,Y)$ are discrete},\\
\displaystyle \int\!\!\!\int g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y, & \text{if $(X,Y)$ are continuous}.
\end{cases}
\]











Definition 1.12 (Moments) The quantities \(\mathrm{E}[X], \mathrm{E}[X^2], \mathrm{E}[X^3], \ldots\) are the (raw) moments of \(X\).











Definition 1.13 (Variance) The population variance of \(X\) is \[
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{E}\!\left[(X-\mathrm{E}[X])^2\right]
= \mathrm{E}[X^2] - \big(\mathrm{E}[X]\big)^2.
\] We often write \(\sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}(X)\). This is a measure of spread.











Definition 1.14 (Standard Deviation) The population standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance: \[
\mathrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}.
\] We often write \(\sigma = \mathrm{SD}(X)\). It shares the same units as \(X\) and measures spread.











Definition 1.15 (Covariance) For two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the covariance is \[
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)
= \mathrm{E}\!\left[(X-\mathrm{E}[X])(Y-\mathrm{E}[Y])\right]
= \mathrm{E}[XY] - \mathrm{E}[X]\mathrm{E}[Y].
\] It measures linear association: positive if \(Y\) tends to increase with \(X\); negative if \(Y\) tends to decrease as \(X\) increases.











Definition 1.16 (Correlation) The correlation (often denoted \(\rho\)) is the scaled covariance \[
\rho = \mathrm{Corr}(X,Y) = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\mathrm{SD}(X)\,\mathrm{SD}(Y)}.
\] Correlation always satisfies \(\rho \in [-1,1]\).











Theorem 1.4 (Independence \(\Rightarrow\) Zero Covariance) If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\).
Note. The converse need not hold: it is possible to have \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\) while \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent.











Example 1.5 (Variance of a Bernoulli Random Variable) A Bernoulli random variable 1.1 \(X\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), with probabilities \[
\operatorname{Pr}(X=1) = p, \qquad \operatorname{Pr}(X=0) = 1-p, \qquad 0 \leq p \leq 1.
\]
For what value of \(p\) is the variance maximised?










TipSolution






Solution 1.5. We compute the mean and variance of \(X\).
\[
\mathrm{E}[X] = 1 \cdot p + 0 \cdot (1-p) = p,
\]
\[
\mathrm{E}[X^2] = 1^2 \cdot p + 0^2 \cdot (1-p) = p.
\]
Therefore, \[
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{E}[X^2] - \big(\mathrm{E}[X]\big)^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p).
\]

To find the value of \(p\) that maximises this variance, consider the function \[
f(p) = p(1-p), \quad 0 \leq p \leq 1.
\]
Differentiate: \[
f'(p) = 1 - 2p.
\]
Setting \(f'(p) = 0\) gives \(p = \tfrac{1}{2}\).
Second derivative: \[
f''(p) = -2 < 0,
\] so this is indeed a maximum.
Finally, check the boundary values: \[
f(0) = 0, \qquad f(1) = 0, \qquad f\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \tfrac{1}{4}.
\]

Conclusion.
The variance of a Bernoulli random variable is maximised at
\[
p = \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad \mathrm{Var}(X) = \tfrac{1}{4}.
\]

WarningNon-Examinable Content



This section provides definitions and results that are used in non-examinable proofs and remarks elsewhere in the notes.
None of the material in this section is examinable.




1.4.1 Convergence of Random Variables







Definition 1.17 (Convergence in Probability) A sequence of random variables \(X_n\) is said to converge in probability to a random variable \(X\) if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\),
\[
\Pr\big(|X_n - X| > \varepsilon\big) \;\longrightarrow\; 0
\quad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\]
We write this as \[
X_n \xrightarrow{p} X.
\]
Intuitively: as \(n\) grows, the probability that \(X_n\) is far from \(X\) becomes negligible.











Definition 1.18 (Convergence in Distribution) A sequence of random variables \(X_n\) is said to converge in distribution to a random variable \(X\) if, for all continuity points \(x\) of \(F_X\),
\[
F_{X_n}(x) \;\longrightarrow\; F_X(x)
\quad \text{as } n \to \infty,
\]
where \(F_{X_n}\) and \(F_X\) are the cumulative distribution functions.
We write this as \[
X_n \xrightarrow{d} X.
\]
Intuitively: the distribution of \(X_n\) “settles down” and approaches that of \(X\).










NoteRelationship



Convergence in probability is stronger than convergence in distribution:
\[
X_n \xrightarrow{p} X \;\;\;\implies\;\;\; X_n \xrightarrow{d} X.
\] But not the other way around.





1.4.2 Probability Inequalities







Proposition 1.1 (Chebyshev’s Inequality) If a random variable \(X\) has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2 < \infty\), then for any \(\varepsilon > 0\),
\[
\Pr\big(|X - \mu| \geq \varepsilon\big)
\;\leq\; \frac{\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}.
\]
This provides a bound on the probability of large deviations from the mean.

2.1 Statistical Inference as “Inverse Probability”
Statistical inference underpins experimental science, machine learning, clinical trials, and more. The overall aim is:
Typical conclusions include estimating a proportion or mean, quantifying uncertainty, comparing groups, or predicting future outcomes.
In probability theory, the usual direction is:
In statistical inference, we reverse the problem:
Formally, we (usually) assume our data are an i.i.d. sample:
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_n \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta).
\]
The goal of statistical inference is to use the observed sample to learn about \(\theta\), and hence about the underlying population.

2  What is Statistical Inference?
text:
2.2 Statistical Models
Whenever we perform statistical inference, we must specify a statistical model.







Definition 2.1 (Statistical Model) A statistical model is a set of candidate population distributions: \[
\mathcal{P}=\{P_\theta \mid \theta\in\Theta\},
\] where \(P_\theta\) is a probability distribution indexed by a parameter \(\theta\), and \(\Theta\) is the parameter space (the set of allowable parameter values).




A statistical model is a working assumption that needs to be checked and verified!







Example 2.1 (Exponential model) Suppose we are interested in modelling waiting times until some event occurs
(e.g. the time between customer arrivals at a service desk).
A simple model is to assume the data are i.i.d. from an exponential distribution: \[
X_i \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda).
\] Write this formally as a statistical model and write down the parameter space.










TipSolution






Solution 2.1. Each data follows the exponential distribution with parameter \(\lambda\). Since \(\lambda > 0\), we have the model: \[
\mathcal{P}=\big\{\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\ \big|\ \lambda>0\big\},
\] with parameter \(\theta=\lambda\) and parameter space1 \[
\Theta = \{\lambda \mid \lambda > 0\} = (0,\infty) = \mathbb{R}^+.
\]
The exponential distribution is often used for modelling the time between events in a Poisson process — situations where events occur continuously and independently at a constant average rate.
For example:
- the time between buses arriving at a stop if buses come at random,
- the time until the next radioactive decay of an atom,
- the waiting time until the next customer enters a shop.
In each case, the exponential model is a natural first assumption.











Example 2.2 (Normal model) Write down the statistical model and the corresponding parameter space used in Section 2.1.1.










TipSolution






Solution 2.2. We assumed the data are i.i.d. Normally distributed with unknown mean and unknown variance: \[
X_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2 \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).
\]
The statistical model is \[
\mathcal{P} = \{ \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2) \mid \mu \in \mathbb{R},\ \sigma^2 > 0 \}.
\]
Here there are two parameters, \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\), which we group into a parameter vector \(\underline{\theta} = (\mu, \sigma^2)\).
The parameter space is2
\[
\Theta = \{ (\mu, \sigma^2) \mid \mu \in \mathbb{R},\ \sigma^2 > 0 \}
       = \mathbb{R} \times (0,\infty)
       = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^+.
\]
The normal model is widely used in practice, for example when data are approximately symmetric and unimodal, such as measurement errors in physics or biological traits like human heights.











Example 2.3 (From words to a model (one-dimensional)) A questionnaire records whether each respondent would recommend a service: “yes” or “no”. Write down a simple model and identify the parameter.










TipSolution






Solution 2.3. Let \(X_i=1\) if respondent \(i\) says “yes”, and \(0\) otherwise.
Model \(X_1,\ldots,X_n \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), where \(p=\Pr(X_i=1)\) is the (unknown) long-run recommendation proportion.
Here \(\theta=p\) and \(\Theta=(0,1)\). The population is all (current/future) potential respondents of interest; the sample is the \(n\) surveyed respondents.











Example 2.4 (A slightly richer example (multinomial)) A bag contains sweets of three colours \(\{\text{red},\text{blue},\text{green}\}\). You draw \(n\) sweets at random with replacement and record counts \((R,B,G)\). Propose a model and name the parameter(s).










TipSolution






Solution 2.4. Model \((R,B,G) \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}\!\left(n;\,p_R,p_B,p_G\right)\) with \(p_R,p_B,p_G\ge 0\) and \(p_R+p_B+p_G=1\).
The parameter is \(\theta=(p_R,p_B,p_G)\), and the parameter space is the 2-simplex \(\Theta=\{(p_R,p_B,p_G)\in[0,1]^3:\sum p_\cdot=1\}\). The population is the long-run distribution of colours produced by the bag; the sample is the observed draws.











Example 2.5 (Image Classification from Machine Learning) In image classification (cat vs not-cat), each training example is a pair \((X_i,Y_i)\) where \(X_i\) is an image and \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\). A generic probabilistic model writes the conditional distribution \[
\mathrm{Pr}_\theta(Y=1\mid X=x)=g_\theta(x),
\] for some function family \(g_\theta\) (e.g. logistic regression or a neural network). What are the sample, population, model, and parameter?










TipSolution






Solution 2.5. 

Sample: the labelled training set \(\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\).

Population: all (future) images and labels of interest.

Model: the family of conditional distributions \(\{ \Pr_\theta(Y=1\mid X=x)=g_\theta(x)\}\).

Parameter: \(\theta\) (e.g. regression co











WarningNon-Examinable Content: Specifying Statistical Models



In this course we focus on how to perform statistical inference once a statistical model has been specified.
We will assume the model is given, and our task is to carry out inference by finding good parameter values using techniques such as:

Parameter Estimation 4
Interval Estimation 7
Hypothesis Testing 9









TipCommon misconceptions and how to avoid them




Parameter \(\neq\) statistic. A parameter \(\theta\) is a property of the population/model (e.g. \(p,\ \mu,\ \sigma^2\)). A statistic (e.g. \(\bar{X}\), a sample proportion) is computed from the sample to learn about \(\theta\).
“Random sample” \(\neq\) “whatever data we found”. The iid assumption is part of the design; convenience samples or dependence can bias inference.
Models are approximations. A model is a useful idealisation, not the truth. Choose \(\mathcal{P}\) sensibly, then check fit later and revise if needed.

title: 2  What is Statistical Inference?
text:
Set notation. There are several equivalent ways to write sets:

Set-builder notation: \(\{\lambda \mid \lambda > 0\}\)

Interval notation: \((0,\infty)\)

Named set: \(\mathbb{R}^+\)

All three describe the same set. In this course, we recommend using set-builder notation when writing statistical models and their parameter spaces.↩︎
Set notation (multiple parameters). When a model has several parameters, it is best to use set-builder notation and collect the parameters into a vector \[
    \underline{\theta} = (\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_p).
  \] The parameter space can then be written as \[
    \Theta = \{(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_p) \mid \theta_1 \in S_1,\ \ldots,\ \theta_p \in S_p\}.
  \]
Here each \(S_j\) is the set of allowed values for parameter \(\theta_j\). To construct \(\Theta\), simply read off the constraints on each parameter from the definition of the distribution (see the Formula Sheet 0.0.0.0.1).
For example, in the Normal model:

\(\mu \in \mathbb{R}\) (any real number),

\(\sigma^2 \in (0,\infty)\) (variance must be positive),

so the parameter space is
\[
    \Theta = \mathbb{R} \times (0,\infty).
  \]
This is called a Cartesian product: we form the parameter space by taking all possible pairs \((\mu, \sigma^2)\) where the first component is from \(\mathbb{R}\) and the second from \((0,\infty)\).
Intuitively, it’s just “all combinations” of the allowed values for each parameter.↩︎

title: 3  Types of Inference
text:
3.1 Philosophies of Inference
Statistical inference is about using a sample to learn about a population. There are two fundamentally different philosophies of inference, and several types of inferential tasks that appear in both.

title: 3  Types of Inference
text:
3.1.1 Frequentist Inference
Frequentist inference is based on the idea of long-run frequency.

The data are considered random, as they represent one possible outcome of repeated sampling from the population.
The parameter \(\theta\) is fixed but unknown.
Inference is about constructing procedures (estimators, tests, intervals) that perform well under repeated sampling.

Preview examples (we will return to these later): the sample mean \(\hat{\mu}\) as an estimator of \(\mu\), a \(t\)-test for comparing means, or a \(95\%\) confidence interval.


3.1.2 Bayesian Inference
Bayesian inference is based on subjective probability as degree of belief.

The data are fixed once observed.
The parameter \(\theta\) is treated as a random variable, with uncertainty described by a prior distribution \(\pi(\theta)\).
Inference updates this prior in light of the data, giving a posterior distribution \(\pi(\theta \mid \text{data})\).

Preview examples (we will return to these later): a posterior mean as an estimator of \(\mu\), a \(95\%\) credible interval, or comparing hypotheses via posterior probabilities.


3.1.3 Key Differences








Perspective
Frequentist Inference
Bayesian Inference




Parameter
Fixed but unknown

Sample
Random (from repeated sampling)
Fixed (once observed)


Probability

Goal

Output

title: 3  Types of Inference
text:
3.2 Inference Tasks
Regardless of philosophy, the core tasks of inference are similar. Suppose we want to infer a parameter \(\theta\) from data:

Point Estimation Give a single “best guess” \(\hat{\theta}\) for the parameter.

Frequentist: choose an estimator with good properties (e.g. unbiasedness).
Bayesian: often the posterior mean, median, or mode.

Interval Estimation Quantify uncertainty in \(\theta\) by reporting a range.

Frequentist: confidence interval
\[
L \leq \theta \leq U
\]
with a given long-run coverage probability.
Bayesian: credible interval, the posterior probability that \(\theta\) lies in \([L,U]\) is, say, 95%.

Hypothesis Testing {#sec-hypothesis-testing-intro} Ask a yes/no question about the parameter \(\theta\). This is done by formalising a claim (the null hypothesis) such as \[
     H_0: \theta \in \Theta_0,
\] and then using the data to judge whether this claim is compatible with the evidence.

Frequentist approach: base the decision on a test statistic and its distribution under \(H_0\), leading to a \(p\)-value or a comparison with a significance level.
Bayesian approach: compare hypotheses using posterior probabilities or Bayes factors, quantifying how much the data shift our beliefs.

Prediction Use data to predict future or unobserved outcomes.

Frequentist: predictive distributions based on sampling models.
Bayesian: posterior predictive distribution, integrating over parameter uncertainty.

title: 4  Frequentist Point Estimation
text:
4.1 Estimators vs. Estimates
A statistic is any function of the sample
\[
T \;=\; T(X_1,\dots,X_n).
\]
Because it is built from the random variables \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), the statistic \(T\) itself is a random quantity: its value varies from sample to sample. Once the data have been observed \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\), plugging them into the same formula produces a single non-random number, which we denote by \(t_{\mathrm{obs}}\) (or simply \(t\)).
When we pick a statistic for the specific purpose of approximating a parameter \(\theta\), we call it an estimator. Its realised value is the estimate.
An estimator is a random variable; an estimate is its realised value.

title: 4  Frequentist Point Estimation
4  Frequentist Point Estimation
text:
4.2 Properties of Estimators
When we use a statistic to estimate a parameter, we want to know how good it is. Three core ideas are bias, variance, and standard error.






TipRemark






Remark 4.2. These properties can often be studied without the full sampling distribution: it is enough to work with moments (expectations/variances) of \(\hat\theta\).





4.2.1 Bias, Variance, and Standard Error







Definition 4.4 (Bias of an Estimator) The bias of an estimator \(\hat{\theta}\) for a parameter \(\theta\) is the difference between its expected value and the true parameter value:
\[
\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta.
\]

If \(\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = 0\), the estimator is called unbiased.
Otherwise, it is biased: it systematically over- or under-estimates \(\theta\).












Example 4.3 (Bias of the Sample Mean) Suppose \(X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with mean \(\mu\).
Show that the sample mean
\[
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
\]
is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu\).










TipSolution






Solution 4.3. We compute the expectation of \(\bar{X}\):
\[
\mathrm{E}[\bar{X}]
= \mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right]
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[X_i].
\]
Since each \(X_i\) has mean \(\mu\),
\[
\mathrm{E}[\bar{X}] = \frac{1}{n}(n\mu) = \mu.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{Bias}(\bar{X})
= \mathrm{E}[\bar{X}] - \mu
= \mu - \mu = 0.
\]
So the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu\).











Definition 4.5 (Variance of an Estimator) The variance measures how much the estimator fluctuates around its expectation:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}])^2\big].
\]
A smaller variance means the estimator is more concentrated and less “noisy.”











Example 4.4 (Variance of the Sample Mean) Suppose \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is a random sample such that \(\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2\).
Show that \[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]










TipSolution






Solution 4.4. Since the data \(X_i\) are independent and have common variance \(\sigma^2\), we have
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X})
= \frac{1}{n^2} \mathrm{Var}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(X_i)
= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
So as \(n\) increases, \(\bar{X}\) becomes more tightly clustered around \(\mu\).











Example 4.5 (Bias of the Sample Variance) Suppose \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is a random sample such that \[
\mathrm{E}[X_i]=\mu \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty.
\] Consider the class of estimators \[
S_c^{2} \;=\; c \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2.
\] Find \(c\) such that \(S_c^{2}\) is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\).










TipSolution






Solution 4.5. 

Note: In the following, we use the fact that, for any random variable \(Y\), \[
\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathrm{E}[Y^2] - \mathrm{E}[Y]^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}[Y^2] = \mathrm{Var}(Y) + \mathrm{E}[Y]^2.
\]

We seek \(c\) such that \(\mathrm{E}[S_c^{2}] = \sigma^2\).
Using the computational identity 4.1, \[
\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2 \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 \;-\; n\,\bar X^{\,2}.
\]
Hence, taking expectations termwise, \[
\mathrm{E}[X_i^2]=\sigma^2+\mu^2,\qquad
\mathrm{E}[\bar X^{\,2}]=\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)+\{\mathrm{E}[\bar X]\}^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\mu^2.
\] Therefore \[
\mathrm{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2\right]
= n(\sigma^2+\mu^2) - n\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\mu^2\right)
= (n-1)\sigma^2.
\] It follows that \[
\mathrm{E}[S_c^{2}] = c\,(n-1)\sigma^2.
\] Unbiasedness \(\mathrm{E}[S_c^{2}]=\sigma^2\) gives \(c=\dfrac{1}{n-1}\).
Conclusion. The unbiased estimator is \[
S^{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2.
\]










TipRemark (Notes on Example 4.5)






Remark 4.3 (Notes on Example 4.5). 

Distributional assumptions. No Normality is required: the conclusion holds for i.i.d. observations with finite variance, \(\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty\).
MLE under Normality. If the data are Normal, the maximum-likelihood estimator is \[
\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2,
\] which is biased downward: \[
\mathrm{E}\!\left[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}\right]=\frac{n-1}{n}\,\sigma^2
\quad\big(\text{bias}=-\sigma^2/n\big).
\] See Example 5.6 for full details.












Definition 4.6 (Standard Error) The standard error of an estimator \(\hat{\theta}\) of \(\theta\), is just the standard deviation of the estimator:
\[
\mathrm{S.E.}(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})}.
\]
It gives a scale for how much we expect the estimator to vary from sample to sample.






4.2.2 Mean Squared Error (MSE)
Bias and variance both matter. The mean squared error (MSE) combines them into a single measure of accuracy.







Definition 4.7 (Error) The error of an estimator is the difference between the estimate and the true parameter:
\[
\mathrm{Error}(\hat{\theta}) = \hat{\theta} - \theta.
\]




However,

The error is random (depends on the sample).
It can be positive or negative (so errors may “cancel out”).

To overcome this, we square the error and take its expectation.







Definition 4.8 (Mean Squared Error (MSE)) The MSE of an estimator \(\hat{\theta}\) of \(\theta\) is
\[
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})=\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big].
\]
This measures the average squared distance between the estimator and the truth.




Directly using this 4.8 can be awkward. A more useful identity decomposes MSE into bias and variance:







Proposition 4.2 (MSE: Bias–Variance Decomposition) For any estimator \(\hat{\theta}\),
\[
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})
= \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2+\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}).
\]










NoteProof






Proof 4.2. Start from the definition:
\[
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})=\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big].
\]
Step 1 (add–and–subtract the mean). Let \(m=\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]\). Then
\[
\hat{\theta}-\theta
=\big(\hat{\theta}-m\big)+\big(m-\theta\big).
\]
Step 2 (expand the square).
\[
(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2
=\big(\hat{\theta}-m\big)^2
+2\big(\hat{\theta}-m\big)\big(m-\theta\big)
+\big(m-\theta\big)^2.
\]
Step 3 (take expectations; use linearity).
\[
\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big]
=\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-m)\!^2\big]}_{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})}
+2\,(m-\theta)\,\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\!\big[\hat{\theta}-m\big]}_{=\,0}
+\underbrace{(m-\theta)^2}_{\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2}.
\]
The middle term vanishes because \(\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}-m]=\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]-m=0\). Hence
\[
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})
=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})+\big(\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]-\theta\big)^2
=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})+\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2.
\]










TipRemark (Why this helps)






Remark 4.4 (Why this helps). 

If \(\hat{\theta}\) is unbiased, then \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})\).
In general there is a bias–variance trade-off: a small intentional bias can reduce variance enough to lower MSE (common in shrinkage/regularised estimators).












Example 4.6 (MSE of Sample Mean) Suppose we have a random sample
\[
X_1,\dots,X_n  \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\underline{\theta})
\]
and we wish to estimate its population mean \(\mu\) with \(\hat{\mu} = c\bar{X}\), where \(c\) is a constant.
Compute the MSE of this estimator.










TipSolution






Solution 4.6. 

Bias:
\[
\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\mu}) = (c-1)\mu.
\]
Variance:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\mu}) = c^2 \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
MSE:
\[
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\mu})
= \frac{c^2\sigma^2}{n} + (c-1)^2 \mu^2.
\]

This shows how a biased estimator can still have low MSE if variance is reduced.











Example 4.7 (MSE of Three Estimators) Suppose that a random variable \(X\) has expected value \(\mathrm{E}[X] = 2\theta\) and variance \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \theta^2\), where \(\theta > 0\) is an unknown parameter.
Another random variable \(Y\), independent of \(X\), has \(\mathrm{E}[Y] = 3\theta\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 2\theta^2\).
Consider the following three estimators of \(\theta\):

\(\hat{\theta}_1 = X/2\),

\(\hat{\theta}_2 = Y/3\),

\(\hat{\theta}_3 = (3X + 2Y)/12\).

Compute the MSE of each estimator, and recommend the best one.










TipSolution






Solution 4.7. We use the rules of expectation and variance for linear functions of random variables (independence of \(X\) and \(Y\) is needed for the variance of \(\hat{\theta}_3\)).

Estimator (i): \(\hat{\theta}_1 = X/2\)

Mean:
\[
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_1] = \frac{\mathrm{E}[X]}{2} = \frac{2\theta}{2} = \theta.
\]
Variance:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_1) = \frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{4} = \frac{\theta^2}{4}.
\]
Since unbiased, \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_1) = \tfrac{\theta^2}{4}\).


Estimator (ii): \(\hat{\theta}_2 = Y/3\)

Mean:
\[
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_2] = \frac{\mathrm{E}[Y]}{3} = \frac{3\theta}{3} = \theta.
\]
Variance:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_2) = \frac{\mathrm{Var}(Y)}{9} = \frac{2\theta^2}{9}.
\]
Since unbiased, \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_2) = \tfrac{2\theta^2}{9}\).


Estimator (iii): \(\hat{\theta}_3 = (3X + 2Y)/12\)

Mean:
\[
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_3] = \frac{3\,\mathrm{E}[X] + 2\,\mathrm{E}[Y]}{12}
= \frac{3(2\theta) + 2(3\theta)}{12} = \theta.
\]
Variance (using independence):
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_3)
= \frac{1}{144}\Big(9\,\mathrm{Var}(X) + 4\,\mathrm{Var}(Y)\Big)
= \frac{1}{144}(9\theta^2 + 8\theta^2)
= \frac{17}{144}\theta^2.
\]
Since unbiased, \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_3) = \tfrac{17}{144}\theta^2\).


Comparison:
- \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_1) = 0.25\theta^2\)
- \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_2) \approx 0.222\theta^2\)
- \(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_3) \approx 0.118\theta^2\)
Thus, \(\hat{\theta}_3\) has the smallest MSE and is the best choice.

title: 4  Frequentist Point Estimation
text:
4.3 Central Limit Theorem (CLT)







Theorem 4.1 (Central Limit Theorem (CLT)) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be an infinite sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with finite mean \(\mu=\mathrm{E}[X_1]\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)<\infty\).
Define the sample mean \[
\bar X_n \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
\] Then, regardless of the original distribution of the \(X_i\), \[
\frac{\bar X_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \;\xrightarrow{\,d\,}\; \mathcal N(0,1)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty.
\]










NoteProof (Not Examinable)






Proof 4.3 (Not Examinable). We do not give a proof here. An outline is provided in separate practice exercises (not examinable).
Note. The notation \(\xrightarrow{d}\) means convergence in distribution: the distribution of the random variable on the left approaches the distribution on the right as \(n\) grows.




The CLT is remarkable: it tells us that whatever the original distribution of the data, the sample mean is approximately Normal for sufficiently large \(n\), and the approximation improves as \(n\) increases.
In practice, for a reasonable sample size we may write \[
\bar X_n \;\overset{approx}{\sim}\; \mathcal N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
\] not only for Normal samples but for many non-Normal populations as well. What counts as “reasonable” depends on how skewed/heavy-tailed the original distribution is; often \(n>20\) suffices, and in many settings even smaller \(n\) will do.
Because \(\bar X_n = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\), the CLT also yields an approximation for sums: \[
\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \;\overset{approx}{\sim}\; \mathcal N\!\left(n\mu,\ n\sigma^2\right).
\]






WarningCommon misconception



The CLT does not say the data become Normal; it says the distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately Normal as \(n\) grows.

title: 4  Frequentist Point Estimation
text:
4.4 Asymptotic Properties of Estimators






Important 4.1: Terminology: Asymptotic in Statistics





An asymptotic property of an estimator is a property that emerges in the limit as the number of observations \(n \to \infty\).
In other words, it describes the large-sample behaviour of an estimator.



So far, we have judged estimators by properties that hold for a fixed sample size \(n\), such as bias 4.4, variance 4.5, and MSE 4.8.
It is also useful to consider how estimators behave when the sample size grows very large.
These are known as the asymptotic (large-sample) properties of estimators.
Formally, suppose we have a random sample
\[
X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n \;\overset{iid}{\sim}\; \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
\]
and a sequence of estimators of \(\theta\) given by
\[
\hat{\theta}_n = g(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n).
\]
We are interested in the properties of \(\hat{\theta}_n\) as \(n \to \infty\). Two fundamental criteria are asymptotic unbiasedness and consistency.







Definition 4.9 (Asymptotic Unbiasedness) We say that \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is asymptotically unbiased for \(\theta\) if
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_n] = \theta.
\]




If an estimator is unbiased for every \(n\), then it is automatically asymptotically unbiased.
However, some biased estimators may still “correct themselves” in the limit and become asymptotically unbiased.







Definition 4.10 (Consistency) An estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is a consistent estimator of \(\theta\) if
\[
\hat{\theta}_n \;\xrightarrow{p}\; \theta
\quad \text{as } n \to \infty,
\]
that is, it converges in probability 1.17 to the true parameter value.




Intuitively, a consistent estimator will “home in” on the true parameter as the sample size grows.
Using Definition 4.10 directly can be tricky. The following gives a sufficient condition that is easier to verify in practice.







Proposition 4.3 (Sufficient Condition for Consistency) An estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) of \(\theta\) is consistent if both the following hold:

\(\hat{\theta}_n\) is asymptotically unbiased, i.e.
\[
\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}_n) \;\to\; 0 \quad \text{as } n\to\infty,
\]
Its variance shrinks to zero:
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n) \;\to\; 0 \quad \text{as } n\to\infty.
\]











NoteProof (Not Examinable)






Proof 4.4 (Not Examinable). Suppose \(\hat{\theta}_n\) satisfies conditions (1) and (2).
For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), by Chebyshev’s inequality 1.1:
\[
\Pr\big(|\hat{\theta}_n - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_n]| \geq \varepsilon \big)
\;\leq\; \frac{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n)}{\varepsilon^2}.
\]
As \(n \to \infty\), the variance term tends to \(0\), so
\[
\hat{\theta}_n - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_n] \;\xrightarrow{p}\; 0.
\]
Meanwhile, \(\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}_n] \to \theta\) by assumption of asymptotic unbiasedness.
Hence,
\[
\hat{\theta}_n \;\xrightarrow{p}\; \theta,
\]
which proves consistency.











Example 4.8 (Consistency of the Sample Mean) Suppose \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2 < \infty\).
Show that \(\bar{X}_n\) is a consistent estimator of \(\mu\).










TipSolution






Solution 4.8. Recall that \[
\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
\]

Bias:
\[
\mathrm{E}[\bar{X}_n] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[X_i] = \mu.
\] Thus \(\bar{X}_n\) is unbiased for all \(n\), hence asymptotically unbiased.
Variance:
Since the \(X_i\) are independent, \[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(X_i)
= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\] As \(n \to \infty\), this variance tends to \(0\).

Therefore, \(\bar{X}_n\) is both unbiased and has variance vanishing as \(n\) grows.
By Proposition 4.3, it is a consistent estimator of \(\mu\).










TipRemark (Consistency)






Remark 4.5 (Consistency). 

Consistency requires convergence in probability 1.17, not necessarily unbiasedness at every finite \(n\).

In this course, you can always use the sufficient condition (Proposition 4.3) to prove consistency.

title: 5  Likelihood
text:
5.1 Likelihoods Under Independence and Dependence
The likelihood function is simply the joint density (or probability mass function) of the observed data:
\[
f(\underline{x} \mid \theta),
\quad \underline{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n).
\]
It plays a central role in both frequentist and Bayesian statistics.
The form of the likelihood depends crucially on whether our observations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), merely independent, or dependent. These three cases look similar but lead to different joint densities.

title: 5  Likelihood
text:
i.i.d. dataIndependent (not identical) dataDependent data


This is the default case in most of this course.
Suppose \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables:
\[
X_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
\quad i = 1, \ldots, n.
\]
Each \(X_i\) has density (or PMF)
\[
f(x \mid \theta).
\]
Then the joint density of the full sample is
\[
f(x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \theta).
\]


If instead the samples are independent but not identically distributed:
\[
X_i \sim \mathrm{Distribution}_i(\theta),
\]
with individual densities \(f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta)\), then the joint density becomes
\[
f(x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta).
\]


In many real-world situations, data are dependent.
Example: Suppose our data are daily temperatures in Newcastle upon Tyne. Yesterday’s temperature will influence today’s temperature, and today’s temperature will influence tomorrow’s.
In such cases, we must model the dependencies explicitly. For instance,
\[
X_{t+1} \mid X_t = x_t  \sim \mathcal{N}(x_t, \sigma^2).
\]
The likelihood is still the joint distribution, but expressed as a product of conditional densities:
\[
f(x_1,\ldots,x_n \mid \sigma^2)
= \prod_{t=1}^n f(x_t \mid x_{t-1}, \sigma^2).
\]
The example above assumed a Markov property (each observation only depends on the previous one). In general, observations may depend on the entire history, in which case the joint density factorises via the chain rule: \[
f(x_1,\ldots,x_n \mid \theta) = f(x_1\mid\theta)\prod_{t=2}^n f(x_t \mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1},\theta)
\]






WarningNon-Examinable Content



This course focuses on the independent case.
Dependent data will be covered in later modules and is not examinable.













Case
Assumption
Factorisation of Joint Density




i.i.d. data
Independent and identically distributed; each with density \(f(x\mid\theta)\)
\(f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid\theta)\)


Independent (not identical) data
Independent; each \(X_i\) may have its own density \(f_{X_i}(x_i\mid\theta)\)
\(f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i\mid\theta)\)


Dependent data (general)
Dependent; factorise using the chain rule
\(f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = f(x_1\mid\theta)\prod_{t=2}^n f(x_t \mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1},\theta)\)









WarningReminder: Non-Examinable Content



The dependent case in the above table is shown for completeness.
This course focuses on the independent case, and the dependent case is not examinable.








TipRemark (Why products?)






Remark 5.1 (Why products?). 

Independence means joint probabilities factorise: \[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \cap B) = \mathrm{Pr}(A) \mathrm{Pr}(B).
\]
By the same rule 1.8, the joint density of independent random variables is the product of their individual densities.
This is a common misconception: without independence, you cannot just multiply.

title: 5  Likelihood
5  Likelihood
text:
5.3 Maximum Likelihood Estimation







Definition 5.2 (Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE)) The MLE is the parameter value \(\hat{\theta}\) that maximises the likelihood function: \[
  \hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \arg \max_{\theta \in \Theta} L(\theta ; \underline{x}).
  \]




Because logs are monotone, it is usually easier to maximise the log-likelihood:
\[
\ell(\theta ; \underline{x}) = \log L(\theta ; \underline{x}).
\]

5.3.1 Computing MLEs







Example 5.3 (Bernoulli MLE) From Example 5.1, we have
\[
L(\theta ; x)
\]
Compute the MLE of \(p\).










TipSolution






Solution 5.1. From the provided likelihood, we first compute the log-likelihood:
\[
\ell(p \mid \underline{x})
= \Big(\sum_i x_i \Big)\log p + \Big(n-\sum_i x_i\Big)\log(1-p).
\] Differentiate and solve: \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial p}\ell(p \mid \underline{x})
= \frac{\sum_i x_i}{p} - \frac{n - \sum_i x_i}{1-p} = 0.
\] This gives \[
\hat{p}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,
\]
the sample proportion of successes.











Example 5.4 (Binomial MLE) Suppose we have a single Binomial 1.2 observation \[
X \sim \textrm{Bin}(n, \theta).
\] Derive its likelihood function.










TipSolution






Solution 5.2. Since we only have one observation, the likelihood function is just the distribution of the observation: \[
L(\theta ; x) = f(x \mid \theta) = \binom{n}{x} \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.
\] The log-likelihood is thus \[
\ell(\theta; x) = \log f(x \mid \theta) = \log\left(\binom{n}{x}\right) + x\log\theta + (n-x)\log(1-\theta).
\] Differentiating2, we obtain \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}
\]











Example 5.5 (Binomial MLE) Suppose we have \(n\) independent Binomial data: \[
X_i \sim \textrm{Bin}(n_i, \theta).
\] Note here that each Binomial data has a different number of Bernoulli trials \(n_i\), which are known.
Derive its likelihood function.










TipSolution






Solution 5.3. The likelihood function is the joint distribution of the \(n\) observations \[
f(\underline{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \binom{n_i}{x_i} \theta^{x_i}(1-\theta)^{n_i - x_i}.
\]











Example 5.6 (Normal MLE for \(\mu\)) Under \[
L(\theta ; x)
\]
Compute the MLE of \(p\).











Tip✨ Big picture:




Likelihood tells us how plausible each parameter value is, given the data.
The MLE chooses the parameter value that makes the observed data most likely.
Later, in Bayesian inference, we will combine the likelihood with a prior distribution on \(\theta\) to obtain a posterior distribution.

6.1 Introduction to the Bayesian approach
As discussed in the course introduction, Bayesian inference takes a different perspective from the frequentist approach:
The randomness here does not mean that the parameter is physically fluctuating — instead, it reflects our uncertainty about its value.

title: 6  Bayesian Inference
text:
In the frequentist view, the parameter \(\theta\) is fixed but unknown.
In the Bayesian view, the parameter \(\theta\) is treated as a random variable.



6.1.1 Why is this useful?
A key advantage of Bayesian inference is that it allows us to incorporate prior information1 about the parameter.







Definition 6.1 (Prior Distribution.) Our uncertainty about \(\theta\) is represented by a probability distribution, called the prior distribution:
\[
\theta \sim \pi(\theta).
\]
Here \(\pi(\theta)\) denotes the prior density (PDF or PMF).











Example 6.1 Suppose \(\theta\) is the average exam score of students in a module. From past experience, the average score tends to be around 60, with most cohorts lying within about 10 marks of this.
We could encode this information as a Normal prior:
\[
\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu=60,\;\sigma^2=10^2).
\]
This prior expresses our belief before seeing the new data.

title: 6  Bayesian Inference
text:
6.2 Bayes’ Theorem
Bayesian inference takes its name from Bayes’ theorem, which tells us how to update our beliefs about \(\theta\) after seeing data.
Recall from probability that for events \(A\) and \(B\):
\[
\mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(B \mid A)\,\mathrm{Pr}(A)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
\]
To generalise this idea to random variables and densities, we use conditional densities:
\[
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f_{XY}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}.
\]






TipRemark






Remark 6.1. Notation. We will usually write \(f(x \mid y)\) rather than \(f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)\) to keep things simple. Both mean the same thing.




Using this, we obtain Bayes’ theorem for densities.







Theorem 6.1 (Bayes’ Theorem for Densities.) For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\):
\[
f(x \mid y) = \frac{f(y \mid x)\,f(x)}{f(y)}.
\]










NoteProof






Proof 6.1. By the definition of conditional density:
\[
f(x \mid y) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f(y)},
\qquad
f(y \mid x) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f(x)}.
\]
Rearranging the second expression gives \(f(x,y) = f(y \mid x) f(x)\). Substituting this into the first gives
\[
f(x \mid y) = \frac{f(y \mid x) f(x)}{f(y)}.
\]

title: 6  Bayesian Inference
text:
6.3 Bayes’ Theorem in Statistics
In Bayesian inference, we apply Bayes’ theorem with:

\(x = \theta\) (the parameter, treated as random),
\(y = \underline{x}\) (the observed data).

This gives:
\[
\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})
= \frac{f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)}{f(\underline{x})}.
\]







Definition 6.2 (Posterior Distribution.) \[
\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})
= \frac{f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)}{f(\underline{x})}.
\]
The posterior combines two ingredients:

The likelihood \(f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)\) (information from the data).
The prior \(\pi(\theta)\) (information before seeing the data).

The denominator \(f(\underline{x})\) is a normalising constant ensuring the posterior integrates to 1.










Important✨ Big picture:



Bayesian inference updates prior beliefs about parameters using the likelihood from the data, producing the posterior distribution which represents updated uncertainty.


Let’s start with a simple example to see how this works:







Example 6.2 (Biased Coin) We consider a possibly biased coin with parameter \(\theta = \Pr(\text{Head})\). Before seeing data, we express no preference over \(\theta\in(0,1)\) via a uniform prior: \[
\theta \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1) \equiv \mathrm{Beta}(1,1), \qquad \pi(\theta)=1 \ \text{for } 0<\theta<1.
\] Hence \(\mathrm{E}[\theta]=0.5\).
We toss the coin \(n=5\) times and observe \(x=1\) head. Find the posterior \(\pi(\theta\mid x)\).










TipSolution






Solution 6.1. Let \(X\) be the number of heads in \(5\) tosses. Assuming that each coin throw is independent and identically distributed, \(X\) is Binomial2: \[
    X \mid \theta \sim \textrm{Bin}(5,\theta).
\] Note that there is only a single observation here: one experiment is “tossing the coin \(5\) times and seeing how many come up heads”. The probability of observing \(X=1\) is \[
    f(x = 1 \mid \theta) = 5\theta(1-\theta)^4
\] If we plot this:
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show code"
#| fig-align: center

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import math

def binom_lik(theta):
    return 5 * theta * (1 - theta) ** 4


theta_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
binom_lik_vals = binom_lik(theta_grid)

plt.figure(figsize=(5,3))
plt.plot(theta_grid, binom_lik_vals)
plt.xlabel(r"$\theta$")
plt.ylabel("Likelihood")
plt.title("Binomial Likelihood (with $n=5$ and $X=1$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  
we see that this favours \(\theta\) around \(0.2\). In fact, in Example 5.4, we saw that the MLE is \(\hat{\theta} = 0.2\).
Our prior for \(\theta\) was \(\pi(\theta) = 1\), for \(0 < \theta < 1\). To update our beliefs, by conditioning on the single observation \(x=2\), we use Bayes Theorem 6.2: \[
    \pi(\theta|x=1)=\frac{\pi(\theta)f(x=1|\theta)}{f(x=1)} = \frac{1 \times 5\theta(1-\theta)^4}{f(x=1)}, \quad 0 < \theta < 1.
\] To compute the denominator, \(f(x=1)\), we use the law of total probability 1.3:
\[\begin{align*}
f(x=1) &=\int_\Theta\pi(\theta)f(x=1\, |\,\theta)\,d\theta = \int_0^1 1\times 5\theta(1-\theta)^4\,d\theta \\
&=\int_0^1 \theta\times 5(1-\theta)^4\,d\theta =\left[-(1-\theta)^5\,\theta\right]^1_0
+\int_0^1 (1-\theta)^5\,d\theta \\
&=0 + \left[-\frac{(1-\theta)^6}{6}\right]^1_0 =\frac{1}{6}.
\end{align*}\]
Therefore, the posterior density is (for \(0<\theta<1\)):
\[\begin{align*}
\pi(\theta|x=1)&=\frac{\pi(\theta)f(x=1|\theta)}{f(x=1)} =\frac{5\theta(1-\theta)^4}{1/6}\\
&=30\,\theta(1-\theta)^4 =\frac{\theta(1-\theta)^4}{\mathrm{B}(2,5)},\quad\quad 0<\theta<1,
\end{align*}\]
and so the posterior distribution is \(\theta|x=1\sim \textrm{Beta}(2,5)\). This distribution has its mode at \(\theta=0.2\), and mean at \(\mathrm{E}[\theta|x=1]=2/7=0.286\).




The main difficulty in calculating the posterior distribution was in obtaining the \(f(x)\) term. However, in many cases we can recognise the posterior distribution without the need to calculate this constant term (constant with respect to \(\theta\)). In this example, we can calculate the posterior distribution as
\[\begin{align*}
\pi(\theta|\underline{x})&\propto\pi(\theta)f(x=1|\theta) \\
&\propto 1\times 5\theta(1-\theta)^4,\quad\quad 0<\theta<1  \\
&=k\theta(1-\theta)^4,\quad\quad 0<\theta<1.
\end{align*}\]
As \(\theta\) is a continuous quantity, what we would like to know is what continuous distribution defined on \((0,1)\) has a probability density function which takes the form \(k\theta^{g-1}(1-\theta)^{h-1}\). The answer is the \(\textrm{Beta}(g,h)\) distribution. Therefore, choosing \(g\) and \(h\) appropriately, we can see that the posterior distribution is \(\theta|x=1\sim \textrm{Beta}(2,5)\).
Summary:
It is possible that we have a biased coin. If we suppose that all values of \(\theta=\text{Pr(Head)}\) are equally likely and then observe 1 head out of 5, then the most likely value of \(\theta\) is 0.2 — the same as the most likely value from the data alone (not surprising!). However, on average, we would expect \(\theta\) to be around 0.286. Uncertainty about \(\theta\) has changed from a (prior) standard deviation of 0.289 to a (posterior) standard deviation of 0.160. The changes in our beliefs about \(\theta\) are more fully described by the prior and posterior distributions shown in Figure 6.1.

Example 6.3 Consider an experiment to determine how good a music expert is at distinguishing between pages from Haydn and Mozart scores. Let \(\theta=\mathrm{Pr}(\text{correct choice})\). Suppose that, before conducting the experiment, we have been told that the expert is very competent. In fact, it is suggested that we should have a prior distribution which has a mode around \(\theta=0.95\) and for which \(\mathrm{Pr}(\theta<0.8)\) is very small. We choose \(\theta\sim \textrm{Beta}(77,5)\), with probability density function \[
\pi(\theta)=128107980\,\theta^{76}(1-\theta)^4,\quad\quad 0<\theta<1.
\] A graph of this prior density is given as follows:

title: 7  Frequentist Interval Estimation
7  Frequentist Interval Estimation
text:
Point Estimate: a single statistic \(\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})\).
Interval estimate: two statistics \(L(\underline{X})\) and \(U(\underline{X})\) that form a random interval.








Definition 7.1 (Confidence Interval) A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\theta\) is a random interval \[
\big[L(\underline{X}),\; U(\underline{X})\big]
\] satisfying \[
\mathrm{Pr} \big(L(\underline{X}) < \theta < U(\underline{X})\big) = 1 - \alpha.
\]
This property is called coverage: in the long run, a proportion \(1-\alpha\) of such intervals (constructed from repeated experiments) will contain the true \(\theta\).















Important 7.1: Terminology: Exact vs. Approximate Confidence Intervals



A confidence interval (CI) is a random interval, constructed from the data, that aims to contain the true parameter value with a specified probability (the coverage probability).

Exact CI. The coverage probability is exactly equal to the nominal level (e.g. \(95\%\)). Such intervals are sometimes called well-calibrated. These are rare, but they can be derived in some classical settings (e.g. certain normal models).
Approximate CI. The coverage probability is only guaranteed asymptotically (typically as \(n \to \infty\)). In practice, most commonly used intervals are of this type.

title: 7  Frequentist Interval Estimation
text:
7.2 Interpreting Confidence Intervals
In practice, we only ever observe one dataset \(\underline{x}\). So we calculate the observed interval: \[
[L_{\text{obs}}, U_{\text{obs}}]
= \big[L(\underline{x}), U(\underline{x})\big].
\]
Once the data are observed, this interval is fixed, not random.
Therefore, a frequentist would not say \[
\mathrm{Pr}(L_{\text{obs}} < \theta < U_{\text{obs}}) = 1 - \alpha.
\] That statement is meaningless, because \(\theta\) is not random in the frequentist view.
Instead, the correct interpretation is: our method has long-run coverage \(1-\alpha\).

title: 7  Frequentist Interval Estimation
text:
7.3 Exact Confidence Intervals
Before turning to specific examples, it is useful to outline the general strategy for constructing an exact confidence intervals 7.1.

7.3.1 General Strategy

Choose an estimator. Start with an estimator \(\hat{\theta}=\hat{\theta}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) for the parameter of interest \(\theta\).
Identify its sampling distribution. For exact intervals, the exact distribution of \(\hat{\theta}\) under the model must be known.
Form a pivotal quantity. Construct a function \(Z=Z(\underline{X},\theta)\) whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameters. Such a \(Z\) is called a pivot.
Use quantiles of the pivot. From the known distribution of \(Z\), find constants \(a,b\) such that
\[
\operatorname{Pr}\!\big(a \leq Z \leq b\big) = 1-\alpha.
\]
Invert the inequalities. Solve \(a \leq Z(\underline{X},\theta) \leq b\) for \(\theta\). The result is an exact \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\theta\).







WarningNon-Examinable Content



This general strategy for constructing exact confidence intervals is not examinable. In particular, you do not need to remember the term pivot.




7.3.2 The Normal Case (Known Variance)
Let’s apply the general strategy 7.3.1 to construct an exact confidence interval for the mean of a normal distribution with known variance.
Suppose we observe a normal random sample:
\[
X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \quad i=1,\dots,n.
\]

Choose an estimator. Use the sample mean:
\[
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
\]
Identify its sampling distribution. Since the \(X_i\) are normal, \[
\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu, \tfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
\]
Form a pivotal quantity. Standardise to remove dependence on \(\mu\):
\[
Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).
\]
Use quantiles of the pivot. For the standard normal,
\[
\Pr\!\left(-z_{1-\alpha/2} \leq Z \leq z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha,
\]
where \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is the \((1-\alpha/2)\) quantile.
Invert the inequalities. Substituting \(Z\) and rearranging gives
\[
\Pr\!\left(\bar{X} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \mu \;\leq\; \bar{X} + z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1-\alpha.
\]

Therefore, an exact \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
\mu \in \Bigl[\bar{X} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \;\; \bar{X} + z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\Bigr],
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\bar{X} \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]






TipRemark (Quantiles of the pivot)






Remark 7.1 (Quantiles of the pivot). When constructing a confidence interval from a pivot, the choice of quantiles is not unique.

In the symmetric case, we use
\[
\Pr\!\left(-z_{1-\alpha/2} \leq Z \leq z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha,
\]
which gives the familiar two-sided interval.
But we could instead use any pair of quantiles \(z_{\alpha_1}, z_{1-\alpha_2}\) with \(\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha\):
\[
\Pr\!\left(z_{\alpha_1} \leq Z \leq z_{1-\alpha_2}\right) = 1-\alpha.
\]
As a special case, a one-sided interval arises from
\[
\Pr\!\left(Z \leq z_{1-\alpha}\right) = 1-\alpha.
\]

The symmetric interval is usually preferred because it places equal probability mass in both tails, making it “balanced” around the estimator. This choice minimises the interval length for symmetric distributions (like the normal), which is why it is standard.











Example 7.1 (Confidence Intervals with Known Variance) An archaeologist found preserved in a peat bog the skeletons of 30 adult males from an unknown human population. She is interested in skeleton lengths.
The sample mean is \(\bar{x} = 161.72\) cm. Assume that the skeleton lengths come from a \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) distribution.
Further, measurements from other human populations at the time suggest that it is reasonable to assume the population variance is \(\sigma^2 = 100 \ \text{cm}^2\).

Construct 95% and 99% confidence intervals for \(\mu\).

How many skeletons would be needed to ensure that the width of a 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is no greater than 4 cm?











TipSolution






Solution 7.1. Step 1. Confidence intervals for \(\mu\).
We have \(\bar{x} = 161.72\), \(n=30\), \(\sigma = 10\).
For a confidence interval, the formula is \[
\bar{x} \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]

For \(95\%\) confidence, \(z_{0.05/2} = 1.96\):
\[
161.72 \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{10}{\sqrt{30}}
= 161.72 \pm 3.578
= (158.14, \ 165.30).
\]
For 99% confidence, \(z_{0.01/2} = 2.576\):
\[
161.72 \pm 2.576 \cdot \frac{10}{\sqrt{30}}
= 161.72 \pm 4.703
= (157.02, \ 166.42).
\]


Step 2. Required sample size for desired width.
The width of a 95% CI is \[
\text{Width} = 2 \cdot z_{0.05/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
= 2 \cdot 1.96 \cdot \frac{10}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
We want this \(\leq 4\): \[
2 \cdot 1.96 \cdot \frac{10}{\sqrt{n}} \leq 4
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
\sqrt{n} \geq \frac{2 \cdot 1.96 \cdot 10}{4} = 9.8.
\]
So \[
n \geq (9.8)^2 = 96.04.
\]
Therefore, at least 97 skeletons are needed.







7.3.3 The Normal Case (Unknown Variance)
Let’s apply the general strategy 7.3.1 to construct an exact confidence interval for the mean of a normal distribution when the variance is unknown.
Suppose we observe a normal random sample with unknown mean and variance:
\[
X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \quad i=1,\dots,n.
\]
Since \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we estimate it using the sample variance 4.2:
\[
S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2.
\]


Aside: The Student’s \(t\) Distribution

Discovered by William Sealy Gosset in 1908, under the pseudonym “Student”.
Defined as
\[
T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/\nu}}, \quad Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \;\; U \sim \chi^2_\nu, \;\; Z \perp U.
\]
Shape is similar to \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) but with heavier tails, reflecting the extra uncertainty from estimating \(\sigma^2\).
As \(\nu \to \infty\), \(t_\nu \overset{d}{\to} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\).



Choose an estimator. Use the sample mean:
\[
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
\]
Identify its sampling distribution. As before,
\[
\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu, \tfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
\]
But now \(\sigma^2\) is unknown and must be estimated by \(S^2\).
Form a pivotal quantity. Standardise using \(S\):
\[
T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}.
\]
It can be shown (using \(\chi^2\) theory and independence between \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\)) that
\[
T \sim t_{n-1}.
\]
Use quantiles of the pivot. For the \(t\) distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom,
\[
\Pr\!\left(-t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2} \leq T \leq t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha,
\]
where \(t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\) is the \((1-\alpha/2)\) quantile.
Invert the inequalities. Substituting \(T\) and rearranging gives
\[
\Pr\!\left(\bar{X} - t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{S}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \mu \;\leq\; \bar{X} + t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1-\alpha.
\]

Therefore, an exact \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
\mu \in \Bigl[\bar{X} - t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{S}{\sqrt{n}}, \;\; \bar{X} + t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{S}{\sqrt{n}}\Bigr],
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\bar{X} \;\pm\; t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]

title: 7  Frequentist Interval Estimation
text:
7.4 Approximate Confidence Intervals
For more general distributions (not necessarily normal), exact CIs are not available. In such cases we rely on asymptotics. For example:

The asymptotic distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator
The central limit theorem.


7.4.1 Large Sample Confidence Intervals

7.4.1.1 Step 1: CLT
If \(\hat{\theta}\) is an estimator of a parameter \(\theta\) with finite variance, then for large \(n\):
\[
\frac{\hat{\theta} - \theta}{\text{SE}(\hat{\theta})} \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}(0,1),
\]
where \(\text{SE}(\hat{\theta})\) is the standard error (the standard deviation of \(\hat{\theta}\)).


7.4.1.2 Step 2: Approximate interval
Therefore, the same logic as in the normal case gives:
\[
\theta \in \biggl[\,\hat{\theta} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\text{SE}(\hat{\theta}), \;\; \hat{\theta} + z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\text{SE}(\hat{\theta}) \,\biggr].
\]
Or equivalently:
\[
\hat{\theta} \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\text{SE}(\hat{\theta}).
\]
This is an approximate \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval, valid asymptotically as \(n \to \infty\).

title: 7  Frequentist Interval Estimation
text: Recall from Chapter 6 that Bayesians do not return a single “best guess,” but a full posterior distribution over parameter values. From this distribution we can compute summaries such as plausible ranges of \(\theta\) (see Chapter 8), which play a role similar to confidence intervals but with a different interpretation.↩︎

title: 8  Bayesian Intervals
text:
8.1 Bayesian Credible Intervals
A more useful summary of the posterior distribution is one which also reflects its variation.
For example, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) Bayesian credible interval for \(\theta\) is any region \(C_\alpha\) that satisfies
\[
\mathrm{Pr}(\theta \in C_\alpha \mid \underline{x}) = 1-\alpha.
\]
If \(\theta\) is a continuous quantity with posterior probability density function \(\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})\) then
\[
\int_{C_\alpha} \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})\,d\theta = 1-\alpha.
\]
The usual correction is made for discrete \(\theta\), that is, we take the largest region \(C_\alpha\) such that \(\mathrm{Pr}(\theta \in C_\alpha \mid \underline{x}) \leq 1-\alpha\).
Clearly these intervals are not unique, since there will be many intervals with the correct probability coverage for a given posterior distribution.
A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) highest density interval (HDI) for \(\theta\) is the region
\[
C_\alpha = \{\theta :~ \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) \geq \gamma \},
\]
where \(\gamma\) is chosen so that \(\mathrm{Pr}(\theta \in C_\alpha \mid \underline{x}) = 1-\alpha\).
This region is sometimes called a most plausible Bayesian credible interval.
If the posterior distribution has many modes, then it is possible that the HDI will be the union of several disjoint regions. For example,
\[
C_\alpha = (a,b)\cup(c,d)\cup(e,f), \quad a<b<c<d<e<f.
\]

title: 8  Bayesian Intervals
text:
8.1.1 Interpretation of confidence intervals
Suppose \(C_B\) is a 95% Bayesian credible interval for \(\theta\) and \(C_F\) is a 95% frequentist confidence interval for \(\theta\). These intervals do not have the same interpretation:

The probability that \(C_B\) contains \(\theta\) is 0.95.

The probability that \(C_F\) contains \(\theta\) is either 0 or 1 (since \(\theta\) does not have a non-degenerate probability distribution).

The interval \(C_F\) covers the true value \(\theta\) on 95% of occasions — in repeated applications of the formula.









Example 8.1 (Beta HDI) Suppose that the posterior distribution for \(\theta\) is a \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,24)\) distribution, with probability density function
\[
\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) = 24(1-\theta)^{23}, \quad 0<\theta<1.
\]
Task. Determine the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) HDI for~\(\theta\).










TipSolution






Solution 8.1. The HDI must include those values of \(\theta\) with highest posterior density and so must take the form \(C_\alpha=(0,b)\). The end-point \(b\) must satisfy
\[
\int_0^b 24(1-\theta)^{23}\,d\theta = 1-\alpha.
\]
Now,
\[
\int_0^b 24(1-\theta)^{23}\,d\theta
= \left[-(1-\theta)^{24}\right]^b_0 = 1-(1-b)^{24}.
\]
Hence,
\[
1-(1-b)^{24} = 1-\alpha
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1-b=\alpha^{1/24}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b=1-\alpha^{1/24}.
\]
Therefore, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) HDI for \(\theta\) is
\[
(0,\, 1-\alpha^{1/24}).
\]












Example 8.2 (Normal HDI) Suppose we have a random sample \(\underline{x}e\) from a \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,1/\tau)\) distribution (where \(\tau\) is known).
We have seen that, assuming vague prior knowledge, the posterior distribution is
\[
\mu \mid \underline{x} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar x,\; \tfrac{1}{n\tau}\right).
\]
Task. Determine the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) HDI for~\(\mu\).










TipSolution






Solution 8.2. This distribution has a symmetric bell shape and so the HDI takes the form \(C_\alpha=(a,b)\) with end-points
\[
a=\bar x - \frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{n\tau}},
\qquad
b=\bar x + \frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{n\tau}},
\]
where \(z_\alpha\) is the upper \(\alpha\)-quantile of the \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) distribution.
Therefore, the 95% HDI for~\(\mu\) is
\[
\left(\bar x - \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{n\tau}},\;
\bar x + \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{n\tau}}\right).
\]
Note that this interval is numerically identical to the 95% frequentist confidence interval for the (population) mean of a normal random sample with known variance.
However, the interpretation is very different.

title: 9  Frequentist Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.1 Formal Setup
Recalling the main inference tasks 3.2, we now move from interval estimation to hypothesis testing.
The name hypothesis testing comes from the scientific method:
If the data are consistent, this provides support for the hypothesis (though never proof). If the data look very unlikely under the hypothesis, this is evidence against it.
Unlike estimation (which gives a range of plausible values), hypothesis testing asks a yes/no question about the parameter \(\theta\).
We formalise this by specifying a null hypothesis \(H_0\), a concrete mathematical statement about \(\theta\):
\[
H_0 : \theta \in \Theta_0,
\]
where \(\Theta_0 \subseteq \Theta\) is part of the parameter space.
We then use the observed data \(\underline{x}\) to evaluate whether \(H_0\) is plausible. The frequentist reasoning is:
Visualisation
Suppose our model is
\[
X_i \mid \gamma \sim \mathcal{N}(200, \gamma),
\]
where \(\gamma\) is the variance.
We want to test whether \(\gamma = 10\). That is:
\[
H_0: \gamma = 10.
\]
The frequentist approach is: assume \(H_0\) is true and then check whether the observed data are typical of a normal distribution with variance \(10\).
n = 30
mu0 = 200       // null mean
sigma = 10      // std deviation under null
alpha = 0.05

// Null sampling distribution

// Compute rejection region bounds

lower = mu0 - 1.96 * sigma/Math.sqrt(n)
upper = mu0 + 1.96 * sigma/Math.sqrt(n)

// Plot
Plot.plot({
  width: 600, height: 300,

    // Null distribution

                                    * Math.exp(-0.5*((x-mu0)/(sigma/Math.sqrt(n)))**2)})), 
              {x:"x", y:"y", stroke: "var(--brand-red)" }),

title: 9  Frequentist Hypothesis Testing
text:
Assume \(H_0\) is true.
Use the statistical model to work out what kinds of data would be typical under \(H_0\).
Compare the actual data with this prediction. If the data look very unusual under \(H_0\), this counts against the hypothesis.

title: 9  Frequentist Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.2 The Testing Procedure
Working directly with the full data distribution can be complicated. Instead, we reduce the data to a test statistic \(T(\underline{X})\) that captures the evidence relevant to \(H_0\).
The general frequentist procedure is:

Choose a test statistic \(T(\underline{X})\) that is sensitive to departures from \(H_0\).
Derive its sampling distribution under \(H_0\).
Compute the observed test statistic \(T_{\text{obs}}\) from the data.
Calculate a \(p\)-value: the probability of observing \(T(\underline{X})\) at least as extreme as \(T_{\text{obs}}\), assuming \(H_0\) is true.
Decision:

If the \(p\)-value is below a chosen threshold \(\alpha\) (the significance level), we reject \(H_0\).
Otherwise, we fail to reject \(H_0\)1.



9.2.1 Types of Errors
Because decisions are based on data (which vary by chance), mistakes are inevitable:

Type I Error: rejecting \(H_0\) when it is actually true.
Type II Error: failing to reject \(H_0\) when the alternative is true.

We will return to these concepts later when discussing test performance and power.

title: 9  Frequentist Hypothesis Testing
text: It is common to say “reject \(H_0\)” when the \(p\)-value is small, and “fail to reject \(H_0\)” otherwise. Both phrases should be interpreted with care: rejecting \(H_0\) does not prove it is false, and failing to reject \(H_0\) does not prove it is true. Instead, hypothesis testing provides a decision rule about whether the data are sufficiently inconsistent with \(H_0\) at a chosen significance level.↩︎

title: 10  Bayesian Hypothesis Testing
text:
10.1 Formal Setup
Recalling the main inference tasks 3.2, we now move from interval estimation to hypothesis testing in the Bayesian framework.
The Bayesian perspective is slightly different from the frequentist one: instead of asking whether data look unlikely under a hypothesis, we ask:
We consider two competing hypotheses:
\[
H_0 : \theta \in \Theta_0,
\qquad
H_1 : \theta \in \Theta_1,
\]
with prior probabilities \(\mathrm{Pr}(H_0)\) and \(\mathrm{Pr}(H_1)\).
After observing data \(\underline{x}\), we are interested in the posterior probabilities:
\[
\mathrm{Pr}(H_0 \mid \underline{x})
\quad \text{vs.} \quad
\mathrm{Pr}(H_1 \mid \underline{x}).
\]

title: 10  Bayesian Hypothesis Testing
text:
10.1.1 Computing Posterior Probabilities
By Bayes’ theorem,
\[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Pr}(H_0 \mid \underline{x})
&= \frac{m_0(\underline{x}) \, \mathrm{Pr}(H_0)}{m(\underline{x})}, \\[6pt]
\mathrm{Pr}(H_1 \mid \underline{x})
&= \frac{m_1(\underline{x}) \, \mathrm{Pr}(H_1)}{m(\underline{x})},
\end{align*}\]
where

\(m(\underline{x}) = m_0(\underline{x})\mathrm{Pr}(H_0) + m_1(\underline{x})\mathrm{Pr}(H_1)\) is the overall marginal likelihood,

\(m_0(\underline{x}) = \int_{\Theta_0} f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)\,\pi_0(\theta)\,d\theta\) is the marginal likelihood under \(H_0\),

\(m_1(\underline{x}) = \int_{\Theta_1} f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)\,\pi_1(\theta)\,d\theta\) is the marginal likelihood under \(H_1\).

Thus the Bayesian procedure directly gives the probabilities of \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) after seeing data.



10.1.2 Bayes Factor
The Bayes factor summarises how strongly the data update our beliefs:
\[
B_{10} = \frac{m_1(\underline{x})}{m_0(\underline{x})}.
\]
It measures how much more (or less) the data support \(H_1\) compared to \(H_0\).
Posterior odds are obtained from prior odds via:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{Pr}(H_1 \mid \underline{x})}{\mathrm{Pr}(H_0 \mid \underline{x})}
= B_{10} \times \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(H_1)}{\mathrm{Pr}(H_0)}.
\]

If \(B_{10} > 1\): the data increase belief in \(H_1\).

If \(B_{10} < 1\): the data increase belief in \(H_0\).




10.1.3 Key Contrast with Frequentist Testing

Frequentist: \(H_0\) is either rejected or not, based on a \(p\)-value.

Bayesian: we compute actual probabilities \(\mathrm{Pr}(H_0 \mid \underline{x})\) and \(\mathrm{Pr}(H_1 \mid \underline{x})\), and report the strength of evidence via the Bayes factor.

This makes Bayesian testing especially appealing when we want to quantify relative support for competing models, rather than just rejecting one.

Visualisation
Suppose our model is
\[
X_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, 10),
\]
and we want to test whether \(\mu = 200\):

\(H_0: \mu = 200\)

\(H_1: \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(200, 25)\) (a vague prior centred on 200)

We compare the likelihood of the observed sample mean under each hypothesis.

n = 30
sigma = 10
mu0 = 200

// Slider for observed sample mean
